The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $(39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-65\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $70\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.01\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $10\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=70\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=70I=70\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.01}=100q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=10\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=10\,\frac{dI}{dt}=10\,\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dq}{dt})=10\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-65\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=70\,\frac{dq}{dt}+100q+10\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+10q=\frac{39}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{13}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+10{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}+B{e}^{-2t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+7(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\, &  \\ +10(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{39}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{13}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-21\alpha +\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(\alpha +21\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =\frac{39}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{13}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-21\alpha +\beta =\frac{39}{10}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ \alpha +21\beta =-\frac{13}{2}\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{5},$ $\beta =-\frac{3}{10}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}+B{e}^{-2t}-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-5t}+B{e}^{-2t}$ is the *transient charge*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is the *steady-state charge*. It governs the charge's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
q(t)≈{q}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state charge, in coulombs, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{5})}^{2}+{(-\frac{3}{10})}^{2}}≈0.36,
$$

rounded to two decimal places.
